flawed_step: To prove the claim you would need some way to bound the chromatic number of a triangle-free graph by 4. For example, you might claim that every triangle-free graph has a vertex of degree at most 3, then colour greedily. That step cannot be justified. Being triangle-free puts no bound on minimum degree: the complete bipartite graph K_{n,n} has minimum degree n and no triangles. In fact, being triangle-free puts no bound on chromatic number at all, so no proof can work.
counterexample: Use the Mycielski construction. Take a graph G with vertices v1..vn. Add new vertices u1..un and w. Join each ui to every neighbour of vi, and join w to every ui. The result, M(G), is still triangle-free. Its chromatic number is also at least χ(G)+1. Here is why: take a proper k-colouring of M(G) and suppose w has colour k. Recolour every vi that has colour k with the colour of ui. This gives a proper (k−1)-colouring of G. Starting from C5 (χ=3), M(C5) is the Grötzsch graph (11 vertices, χ=4). M(Grötzsch) has 23 vertices, is triangle-free and has χ=5, so it is not 4-colourable.
assessment_summary: The statement is false. A proof attempt fails right away, because being triangle-free does not bound chromatic number. Applying the Mycielski construction twice to C5 gives a 23-vertex triangle-free graph with chromatic number 5, so it is not 4-colourable.
